Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
A multiligamentous knee injury (MLKI) is commonly defined as a high-grade tear of at least two
of the four major knee ligament complexes: the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), the posterior
cruciate ligament (PCL), the posterolateral corner (PLC), and the posteromedial corner (PMC).

Overview
Historically, MLKIs were caused by high-energy trauma that resulted in a knee
dislocation. Improved modern diagnostic tools show that low-energy and high-energy
mechanisms may cause MLKIs. Low-energy trauma may result in MLKIs in patients with
obesity, often referred to as ultra–low-velocity MLKIs.1,2 A bicruciate ligament injury or
an MLKI involving three or more ligaments should be considered a spontaneously
reduced knee dislocation.3 A knee dislocation should be considered a limb-threatening
injury, and careful monitoring of vascular status postinjury is imperative.
Epidemiology
Knee dislocations are reported to constitute 0.02% to 0.2% of all orthopaedic injuries.4,5

Epidemiology
The true incidence of knee dislocation is unknown because the diagnosis of knee
dislocations may be a challenge, and some knee dislocations may be misdiagnosed
because approximately 50% are reported to reduce before presentation.3 Historically,
knee dislocations have been associated with high-energy trauma, such as motor vehicle
collisions, falls from height, and farm and industry injuries. MLKIs not caused by knee
dislocations are more common than previously reported. Recent studies have reported
that 44% to 47% of MLKIs are caused by sporting injuries.6,7 Given the growing burden of
obesity globally, surgeons must be aware of ultra–low-velocity knee dislocations and

Associated Injuries
The rate of associated injuries to other vital organs, such as the head, chest, abdomen, or a
combination of these, has been reported to be 27% in patients who sustain high-energy
trauma.

Associated Injuries
Fractures also are commonly associated with knee dislocations, reported in 50% to 60%
of patients; and the rate of multiple fractures has been reported to be 41% in patients
with high-energy injuries.6 17% to 58% of patients with a knee dislocation have a risk of
ipsilateral limb fracture.8,9 Patients with bilateral MLKIs have a higher risk of
concomitant head, chest, and abdominal injuries compared with patients who have a
unilateral multi-ligamentous knee injury and a similar mechanism of injury.10
Concomitant meniscal and cartilage injuries are common in patients with a MLKI (37.3%

Injury Classification
The term MLKI occasionally has been used interchangeably with the term knee dislocation;
however, not all MLKIs are caused by knee dislocations. Knee dislocations often result in
MLKIs.

Injury Classification
The most widely used classification system was described by Schenck in 1994 and later
modified by Wascher. This classification system is based on the anatomic pattern of
ligament injury and includes associated injuries, such as neurovascular and fracture
injuries (Table 2). The Schenk classification is not predictive of a surgical management
strategy according to a study by Maxwell et al.13 Although approximately 50% of knee
dislocations spontaneously reduce immediately postinjury, a dislocated knee may be
observed in the emergency department. Therefore, surgeons must be able to reduce the
knee to decrease the risk of neurovascular injuries and other soft-tissue complications.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
The acuity of presentation will and should determine the need for urgent assessment and use
of advanced trauma life support protocol to ensure life, followed by limb-saving management.
After the patient is stabilized, a thorough history and physical examination/secondary survey
of the injured limb may proceed.

Patient History
Patients often have a history of trauma and deformity of the knee. A high index of
suspicion for a reduced knee dislocation should accompany any knee injury that involves
three or more ligaments. The mechanism of injury, the position of the knee at the time
of injury, and the timing of the injury are crucial factors. A history of previous knee injury
and current function, as well as age, activity level, and previous surgery or other injuries
also are relevant.
Physical Examination
In patients with high-energy injuries, the first step involves performing Advanced Trauma Life
Support protocol and a general physical examination to rule out other life-threatening injuries.


Physical Examination
All patients with high-energy injuries should be evaluated for a potential MLKI. The
clinician should conduct a serial neurovascular evaluation. Assess for a dimple sign on
the medial aspect of the knee; this may suggest an irreducible knee secondary to
interposition of the medial collateral ligament (MCL) and medial soft-tissue structures.
Swelling and bruising should be assessed. Physical examination of the extensor
mechanism should be performed to rule out disruption; this may include direct
palpation, straight-leg-raise, and active extension from a flexed position if appropriate.
Range of motion (ROM) should be evaluated. Testing ligamentous stability is critical;
however, it may be hampered by soft-tissue swelling, pain, and guarding. This will be
affected by the acuity of presentation. Table 1 shows important clinical tests.
Neurovascular Examination
Vascular examination is critical in an acutely dislocated knee.

Neurovascular Examination
Serial examination of distal pulses should be performed, and the findings should be
compared with those of the contralateral uninjured side. Presence of a pulse does not
exclude vascular injury. Geniculate arteries may provide collateral flow, and palpable
pulses may mask a limb-threatening vascular injury. Vascular assessment should include
palpation of the posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis arterial pulses bilaterally and
evaluation for potential differences in skin color and capillary filling. An absent distal
pulse warrants emergent consultation with vascular surgery, appropriate imaging
studies, and surgical management. A vascular injury in a patient with a knee dislocation
is a limb-threatening injury and must be corrected within 6 to 8 hours to avoid
amputation.
If the distal pulses are asymmetric or diminished, the ankle-brachial index (ABI) should
be obtained. This is done by measuring the systolic blood pressure in the ipsilateral foot

PCL Injuries

PCL Injuries
Bilateral kneeling radiographs may be obtained, or a stress device may be used. A
posterior translation side-to-side difference of 0 to 7 mm usually is observed in patients
with a partial PCL tear. A side-to-side difference of 8 to 11 mm is associated with a
complete isolated PCL tear. A side-to-side difference of more than 12 mm usually is
observed in patients with a complete PCL tear and an additional ligament injury (usually
the PLC or PMC) but also may be seen in patients with decreased sagittal plane tibial
slope.17
PLC Injury

PLC Injury
A side-to-side lateral gapping difference of 2.7 to 4.0 mm represents a complete FCL
tear. A side-to-side difference greater than 4 mm represents a complete PLC injury.18
Bilateral varus stress radiographs are obtained with the knees flexed 20° to 30° (Figure
6). Lateral gapping is assessed by measuring the shortest distance between the
subchondral bone surface of the most distal aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and
the corresponding tibial plateau.

Management
Overview
In patients with a MLKI that presents as a knee dislocation, emergent closed reduction and
splinting or bracing should be performed immediately. Postreduction radiographs should be
obtained to confirm knee reduction.

Overview
Repeat radiographs should be obtained in patients with a posterior knee dislocation who
are awaiting surgical treatment because gravity may cause additional posterior tibial
translation. If reduction cannot be maintained in a brace or splint, an external fixator
may be indicated. Vascular injuries should be addressed emergently; proper imaging via
CT angiography should be performed, and vascular surgeons should be consulted.
Surgical management currently is considered the standard of care; however, the timing
of management currently is a subject of debate. Nonsurgical treatment may be
considered in patients with other life-threatening injuries or in whom surgical treatment
is contraindicated because of comorbidities.
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
With current reconstruction techniques, usually reserved for elderly low-demand patients or
patients with comorbidities that may increase perioperative surgical risk
Patient preference for nonsurgical treatment
Partial or incomplete MLKI resulting in reasonable knee stability
Patients unwilling or unable to follow postoperative activity restrictions or rehabilitation
Early nonsurgical management to re-establish ROM, reduce swelling, and optimize patients
before delayed definitive surgical treatment

Techniques/Procedures
Closed reduction techniques: Similar to most joint dislocations, the in-line traction and
exaggeration of deformity followed by application of force opposite to the mechanism of injury
is recommended.
Bracing/splinting

Nonsurgical Management
Brace may be applied and initially held in extension. Protection against a fixed flexion
deformity is essential. AP and lateral radiographs should be obtained to confirm
maintenance of reduction. Within 1 week postinjury, ROM may be initiated with the use
of a brace to reduce the risk of joint stiffness. A cast also may be used temporarily to
maintain reduction but is associated with the disadvantage of not allowing ROM.
Surgical Management
Indications
Injury of two or more ligaments that results in an unstable knee
Inability to perform activities of daily living because of knee instability
Associated fractures requiring stable fixation
Emergent surgical indications: irreducible knee dislocation requiring open reduction, open
dislocation, vascular injury, or compartment syndrome
Contraindications
Inability to comply with the postoperative rehabilitation protocol
Other medical comorbidities that preclude surgical management

Timing of Surgical Management
Currently, high-level evidence on the optimal timing and approach for the surgical
management of MLKIs is lacking.20-22 Therefore, surgeon experience and surgical ability may
dictate the timing and approach for surgical management. Surgical management may be
performed acutely or in a staged fashion (Videos 1 and 2). The preference of the authors of
this lesson is outlined below
Management of all injured structures in the acute phase (<2 to 3 weeks); however, may be
delayed in patients with vascular and/or skin injuries.
Single-stage reconstruction of all injured structures to restore knee kinematics, enable early
mobilization and rehabilitation, and avoid overloading the reconstructed ligaments
In patients with concomitant lateral-side injuries, acute reconstruction is recommended,
preferably within 2 weeks of injury and definitely within 3 weeks before tissue scarring, which
makes dissection difficult.
Reconstruction of the PLC is recommended because high-grade lateral injuries do not heal
well
Low-grade MCL injuries in combination with a single cruciate ligament tear can be initially
managed with the use of a brace, with possible reconstruction of the cruciate ligament at a
later stage.
Bicruciate ligament injuries with or without concomitant collateral ligament injuries should
be manage early and in a single stage if possible.

Chronic Injuries
Some patients present in a chronic phase because of delayed diagnosis, previous attempts at
nonsurgical treatment, or concomitant fractures or vascular injuries.

Chronic Injuries

these patients. During arthroscopy for multiligament knee surgery, the surgeon should
be cognizant of pump pressure and monitor the leg compartments for fluid
extravasation and possible compartment syndrome. Waiting 7 to 10 days postinjury
before attempting surgical management often is advised to allow for healing of the
capsular injury often associated with MLKI. The use of gravity flow will decrease the risk
of extravasation but may result in compromised visualization.
Foot/ankle contractures should be suspected in patients with a peroneal nerve injury
and can be prevented with the use of an ankle-foot orthosis if peroneal nerve palsy
results in a footdrop. Missed PLC injuries are associated with failed ACL and PCL surgical
management. Any patient with a bicruciate or PCL injury should be examined with a high
index of suspicion for such injuries. If feasible, all pathology should be addressed during
a single surgical procedure. In chronic cases, limb alignment should be assessed so it can
be addressed before or at the time of reconstruction to prevent graft failure.

A open posterolateral and/or posteromedial surgical approach is performed before
arthroscopy to allow for improved soft-tissue visualization and to limit fluid
extravasation into the surgical site. Ligament attachment footprints are identified and
marked for tunnel placement. Tunnel length and diameter are planned to minimize the
risk of convergence and failure. Sockets and tunnels for cruciate ligaments are reamed
first because it is more difficult to change tunnel orientation for these ligaments than for
collateral ligaments. Guide pins for collateral ligaments are placed and visualized with
the use of an arthroscope to ensure no tunnel convergence occurs. Use of a C-arm
should be considered after guide pin placement and before reaming.
Aiming the sMCL tunnel 40° anteriorly and 20° to 40° proximally and the POL tunnel 20°
anteriorly and proximally minimizes the risk of tunnel convergence. 35° to 40° of
angulation in the axial plane and 0° of angulation in the coronal plane (35° to 40°
anteriorly) for FCL and popliteal femoral tunnels is safe and avoids tunnel convergence.
All tunnels (sockets) should be reamed before grafts are passed. Leaving passing sutures
after drilling each tunnel facilitates later graft passage. The recommended graft
tensioning sequence is PCL, ACL, FCL, popliteus, and MCL. Nonanatomic placement of
the tunnels (sockets) may jeopardize the reconstruction; therefore, the tunnels should
be reamed only after verifying the guide-pins are in the correct position. Tunnel
convergence may damage graft and fixation, leading to failure. Passing grafts before all
tunnels are reamed may make visualization difficult and increases the risk of graft or
fixation damage. Tensioning and fixing the collaterals first increases the risk of rotating
the tibia and altering knee kinematics and loading. Tensioning the ACL first subluxates
the tibia posteriorly. A brace should be used postoperatively to protect the grafts and
allow for early ROM. Early rehabilitation is important to regain function and minimize the
risk of joint stiffness.
